pos: n. (the measure of a thing through its depth; recorded of the temple pillars, the brasen sea, and the walls of Ezekiel's house)
etymology: From thick — Old English thicce — with -ness. The Hebrew at Jeremiah 52:21 is obi, thickness, from abah, to be dense; at Ezekiel 41:9 the word is rochab, breadth, of a wall measured through.
biblical_def: Scripture records dimensions with a precision that surprises readers who expect devotional literature. Of the temple pillars carried off to Babylon: “the height of one pillar was eighteen cubits; and a fillet of twelve cubits did compass it; and the thickness thereof was four fingers: it was hollow” (Jeremiah 52:21). Jeremiah is writing an inventory of the plunder, and he gives the wall thickness of a bronze column that no longer stood. Ezekiel's visionary temple is measured the same way: “The thickness of the wall, which was for the side chamber without, was five cubits” (Ezekiel 41:9), and the chambers themselves were built “in the thickness of the wall of the court toward the east” (Ezekiel 42:10). Eight chapters of Ezekiel are given to these measurements. The reason is stated back at the tabernacle: “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exodus 25:40). Nothing in the house of God was left to the builder's discretion, down to the four fingers of bronze in a pillar's wall, because the house was a copy of a pattern and a copy is measured against its original.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thickness as the measure of a body through its depth, opposed to length and breadth — and also density or closeness of parts.
webster_full: THICKNESS, n. The extent of a body from side to side, or from surface to surface; as the thickness of a tree; the thickness of a board.
2. The state of being thick or dense; density; consistence.
3. The state of being close, or of standing near together.
THICK, a. Dense; not thin; as thick vapors.
CUBIT, n. In Scripture and ancient measures, the length of a man's arm from the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger.
scriptures: Jeremiah 52:21
And concerning the pillars, the height of one pillar was eighteen cubits; and a fillet of twelve cubits did compass it; and the thickness thereof was four fingers: it was hollow.
Ezekiel 41:9
The thickness of the wall, which was for the side chamber without, was five cubits: and that which was left was the place of the side chambers that were within.
Ezekiel 42:10
The chambers were in the thickness of the wall of the court toward the east, over against the separate place, and over against the building.
Exodus 25:40
And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount.
corruption_summary: Measurement chapters are skipped as lifeless, and the doctrine they carry — that worship is by pattern and not preference — goes unread with them.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 40 to 48, Exodus 25 to 31 and 35 to 40, and the temple chapters of 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles form one of the largest blocks of Scripture that most Christians never read. The usual explanation is that they are dry, and they are, if a reader wants narrative. What they teach is not dry at all. Every cubit in them is there because God specified it, and the specification is the point: after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount. Hebrews takes that verse and builds on it the doctrine that the earthly sanctuary was the example and shadow of heavenly things — a doctrine impossible to state if the measurements had been left to Bezaleel's taste.

The practical consequence is the regulative principle of worship. If God cared about the thickness of a pillar's wall, the claim that He is indifferent to how He is now approached is not tenable. What Scripture commands in worship is required; what it has not commanded is not permitted. That principle is not derived from a single proof text but from the whole weight of these chapters, from Nadab and Abihu who offered strange fire He commanded not, and from Uzzah who steadied the ark on a cart that should never have been built. The measurements are a long argument, and skipping them costs the conclusion.
roots_summary: Hebrew obi, thickness — Jeremiah 52:21; abah, to be dense; rochab, breadth — Ezekiel 41:9; tabnith, pattern — Exodus 25:40.
roots_lines: Hebrew obi — thickness, density; Jeremiah 52:21 of the hollow bronze pillar.
Hebrew abah — to be thick or dense; the root of the noun.
Hebrew rochab — breadth; Ezekiel 41:9, of a wall measured through.
Hebrew tabnith — pattern, model, structure; Exodus 25:40 and 1 Chronicles 28:19.
Hebrew ammah — a cubit; the standard unit throughout the measurement chapters.
usage: “The thickness thereof was four fingers: it was hollow” — an inventory of plunder, precisely kept.
“The chambers were in the thickness of the wall” — eight chapters of measurement in Ezekiel.
“After their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” — why the cubits are recorded.

pos: n. (magnitude, bulk; in the Authorized Version always of things deliberately made uniform — curtains, cherubim, and the ten bases of the temple)
etymology: From Old French sise, a shortened form of assise, an assize or fixed regulation — hence a settled standard of magnitude. The Hebrew at Exodus 36:9 is middah, a measure; at 1 Kings 6:25 the phrase is middah achath ve-qetseb echad, one measure and one cut.
biblical_def: Every occurrence of size in the Authorized Version describes something made deliberately identical to something else. The tabernacle curtains: “The length of one curtain was twenty and eight cubits, and the breadth of one curtain four cubits: the curtains were all of one size” (Exodus 36:9), and the goats' hair curtains likewise “were of one size” (Exodus 36:15). The cherubim over the ark in Solomon's house: “both the cherubims were of one measure and one size” (1 Kings 6:25). The ten bases for the lavers: “all of them had one casting, one measure, and one size” (1 Kings 7:37). The English word itself descends from assize, a fixed regulation, and that is exactly the sense here — not bulk but conformity to a settled standard. A tabernacle whose curtains varied would not hang; cherubim of different heights would not spread their wings evenly over the mercy seat; ten bases cast to ten patterns would not be interchangeable in the courts. Uniformity in the house of God is functional before it is symbolic, and it is symbolic too, because it is uniformity to a pattern given from above and not agreed among the workmen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) derives size from assize, a settled quantity or allowance, and defines it as bulk, magnitude, or comparative magnitude.
webster_full: SIZE, n. A quantity or portion allotted or assized; hence, bulk, largeness, magnitude.
2. A settled quantity or allowance. In the universities of England, a portion of bread and beer.
3. Figuratively, condition; rank; character; as, men of the same size.
SIZE, v.t. To adjust or arrange according to size or bulk.
ASSIZE, n. An ordinance regulating the weight and measure of things vendible.
scriptures: Exodus 36:9
The length of one curtain was twenty and eight cubits, and the breadth of one curtain four cubits: the curtains were all of one size.
Exodus 36:15
The length of one curtain was thirty cubits, and four cubits was the breadth of one curtain: the eleven curtains were of one size.
1 Kings 6:25
And the other cherub was ten cubits: both the cherubims were of one measure and one size.
1 Kings 7:37
After this manner he made the ten bases: all of them had one casting, one measure, and one size.
corruption_summary: Uniformity in worship is now heard as an insult to individuality, and the tabernacle's one-size curtains are read as a stifling of expression.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of the age is that sameness is deadening and self-expression is the higher good, and this instinct arrives in the church as an argument that every congregation and every worshipper should approach God in whatever manner is authentic to them. The tabernacle chapters answer flatly. God gave a pattern with fixed dimensions, and the men who built it were filled with the Spirit for the work — Bezaleel is the first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the Spirit's gift to him was skill to execute someone else's design exactly. Creativity is not opposed to conformity here; the whole artistry of the tabernacle is conformity beautifully accomplished.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that unity in the church is a unity of standard, not of temperament. The New Testament says there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and it also says the body has many members with different offices. The curtains were all of one size and they were made of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen with cherubim of cunning work. Sameness where God has spoken and liberty where He has not is the old rule, and it is the opposite of both the tyranny that regulates what God left free and the licence that improvises where He has commanded.
roots_summary: Hebrew middah, a measure — Exodus 36:9, 1 Kings 6:25; qetseb, a cut or shape — 1 Kings 6:25; echad, one — the repeated word in every occurrence.
roots_lines: Hebrew middah — a measure, dimension; Exodus 36:9 and 1 Kings 7:37.
Hebrew qetseb — a cut, shape, or form; rendered size at 1 Kings 6:25.
Hebrew echad — one; “one measure, one size, one casting.”
Hebrew mutsaq — a casting; 1 Kings 7:37, all ten bases from one mould.
Old French assise — a fixed regulation; the origin of the English word, and its sense here.
usage: “The curtains were all of one size” — a tabernacle whose curtains varied would not hang.
“Both the cherubims were of one measure and one size” — over the mercy seat.
“One casting, one measure, and one size” — ten bases interchangeable in the courts.

pos: n. (a fixed proportion or daily allotment; the manna gathered “a certain rate every day”, the tribute Solomon received year by year, and the captive king's daily portion)
etymology: From Latin rata, in the phrase pro rata parte, according to a reckoned share, from reri, to reckon. The Hebrew is generally debar yom be-yomo, the matter of a day in its day — a phrase the Authorized Version renders variously as rate, portion, or due.
biblical_def: Scripture measures a great deal by the day. The manna was given so: the people were to “gather a certain rate every day” (Exodus 16:4), and the stated reason is a test — that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no. Enough for the day and no hoarding is a hard discipline, and Israel failed it in the first week. The same phrase governs the temple offerings: Solomon offered “after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts” (2 Chronicles 8:13). Worship was calendared and proportioned, not left to occasion. The word also measures tribute: the nations brought Solomon presents “a rate year by year” (1 Kings 10:25). And it closes the book of Kings on an unexpected note of mercy: Jehoiachin, released from a Babylonian prison, was given “a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life” (2 Kings 25:30). The last recorded fact about the house of David before the exile ends is that its heir was being fed daily at a pagan table.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rate as the proportion or standard by which quantity or value is adjusted, and also a settled allowance of provisions.
webster_full: RATE, n. The proportion or standard by which quantity or value is adjusted; as, to buy at a low rate.
2. Price or amount stated or fixed on any thing.
3. Settled allowance of provisions; ration.
4. Degree; comparative height or value.
RATE, v.t. To set a certain value on; to value at a certain price or degree of excellence.
scriptures: Exodus 16:4

Then said the LORD unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no.
2 Chronicles 8:13

Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.
1 Kings 10:25
And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and armour, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year.
2 Kings 25:30
And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
corruption_summary: Daily dependence is treated as a failure of planning, and the manna test — enough for the day, nothing hoarded — is read as poetry.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 16:4 says the daily rate was a test, and the thing tested was whether Israel would live by God's arrangement rather than their own. Some gathered more and it bred worms; some went out on the seventh day and found nothing. The instinct the manna exposed is universal and is not cured by prudence — Scripture praises the ant that provideth her meat in the summer, and the same Scripture forbids the barn-building of the rich fool. The distinction is not between saving and not saving but between a man whose security rests on the store and a man whose security rests on the God who gives day by day. Our Lord put the manna into the prayer He taught: give us this day our daily bread.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is one of practical unbelief, and it is at least as common in careful, provident people as in careless ones. The principle to recover is the rhythm. Scripture proportions worship by the day, the week, the month, and the year — the daily offering, the sabbath, the new moon, the three feasts — and a religion that operates only in bursts of intensity has abandoned that pattern. The final verse of 2 Kings is the quiet proof that God keeps His own rate: a captive son of David, fed every day at the table of the king who destroyed his city, and the line preserved to Matthew 1.
roots_summary: Hebrew debar yom be-yomo, the matter of a day in its day — Exodus 16:4, 2 Chronicles 8:13, 2 Kings 25:30; mishpat, a due or ordinance — 1 Kings 10:25.
roots_lines: Hebrew debar yom be-yomo — literally “a day's matter in its day”; the standing phrase for a daily allotment.
Hebrew aruchah — an allowance or ration; 2 Kings 25:30 of Jehoiachin's portion.
Hebrew man — manna, so named from the question “what is it?”; Exodus 16.
Hebrew nasah — to test or prove; Exodus 16:4, the stated purpose of the daily rate.
Latin rata, a reckoned share, from reri, to reckon — the source of the English word.
usage: “Gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them” — the manna was a test.
“After a certain rate every day” — worship calendared, not occasional.
“A daily rate for every day, all the days of his life” — the last verse of Kings.

pos: n. (what is left over; in the law of offerings, the portion whose handling was strictly regulated because the thing left was holy)
etymology: From Old French remaindre, from Latin remanere, to stay behind. The Hebrew at Leviticus 6:16 is yether or nothar, that which remains over; nothar specifically names the leftover of a sacrifice, a term with its own body of law.
biblical_def: A sacrifice did not end at the altar; what remained was governed by statute. Of the consecration offering: “if ought of the flesh of the consecrations, or of the bread, remain unto the morning, then thou shalt burn the remainder with fire: it shall not be eaten, because it is holy” (Exodus 29:34). The reason given for the destruction is the holiness of the thing, not its spoiling. Of the meat offering: “the remainder thereof shall Aaron and his sons eat: with unleavened bread shall it be eaten in the holy place” (Leviticus 6:16) — here the leftover is the priests' food, and the place of eating is specified. Of the peace offering brought as a vow: it “shall be eaten the same day… and on the morrow also the remainder of it shall be eaten” (Leviticus 7:16), but “the remainder of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burnt with fire” (Leviticus 7:17). The penalty for ignoring the limit is severe: on the third day it shall not be accepted, it shall not be imputed to him that offered it, it is an abomination, and the soul that eats it shall bear his iniquity (Leviticus 7:18). A right offering wrongly finished was counted as no offering at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines remainder as anything left after the separation and removal of a part, the residue, and in law an estate limited to take effect after another.
webster_full: REMAINDER, n. Any thing left after the separation and removal of a part.
The remainder of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burnt with fire. Lev. 7.
2. The body which remains after the death of a part; relics.
3. In law, an estate limited to take effect and be enjoyed after another estate is determined.
REMAIN, v.i. To continue in a place; to abide; to be left after others have withdrawn.
scriptures: Exodus 29:34
And if ought of the flesh of the consecrations, or of the bread, remain unto the morning, then thou shalt burn the remainder with fire: it shall not be eaten, because it is holy.
Leviticus 6:16
And the remainder thereof shall Aaron and his sons eat: with unleavened bread shall it be eaten in the holy place; in the court of the tabernacle of the congregation they shall eat it.
Leviticus 7:17
But the remainder of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burnt with fire.
Leviticus 7:18

And if any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings be eaten at all on the third day, it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be imputed unto him that offereth it: it shall be an abomination, and the soul that eateth of it shall bear his iniquity.
corruption_summary: The sacrificial law is explained away as primitive food hygiene, which removes both the holiness that governs it and the doctrine of imputation stated in its penalty clause.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often suggested that these regulations are ancient public-health measures in religious dress — that meat kept three days in that climate was dangerous, and the priests knew it. The texts give a different reason and give it plainly: it shall not be eaten, because it is holy. Nor does the hygienic theory account for the rule's structure. Meat from a vow offering might be eaten on the second day and not the third, which no bacteriology recognises; the peace offering of thanksgiving had to be eaten the same day, though it was no more perishable. These are boundaries of holiness, marking that the offering belonged to God and was released for a stated span on stated terms.

Leviticus 7:18 contains one of the most theologically loaded sentences in the sacrificial law: it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be imputed unto him that offereth it. The vocabulary of imputation and acceptance — the very language Paul takes up in Romans 4 concerning Abraham's faith counted for righteousness — is already operating here in the law of leftovers. An offering was not a transaction completed at the moment of slaughter; it was reckoned to the offerer, or not reckoned, and the reckoning could be forfeited by a disobedience after the fact. That is why the Reformed have always read the ceremonial law as a schoolmaster: it teaches, in commodities and days, the categories the gospel later fills with Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew nothar, that which is left of a sacrifice — Leviticus 7:17; yathar, to remain over — the root; chashab, to reckon or impute — Leviticus 7:18.
roots_lines: Hebrew nothar — the leftover of a sacrifice, a technical term of the law; Exodus 29:34 and Leviticus 7:17.
Hebrew yathar — to remain, be left over; the root behind nothar and yether.
Hebrew chashab — to reckon, impute; Leviticus 7:18, and Genesis 15:6 of Abraham's faith.
Hebrew ratsah — to be accepted with favour; the verb denied in Leviticus 7:18.
Hebrew piggul — an abomination, refuse of a sacrifice; the verdict on the third-day flesh.
usage: “Thou shalt burn the remainder with fire: it shall not be eaten, because it is holy” — the reason given.
“The remainder thereof shall Aaron and his sons eat” — the priests' portion, in the holy place.
“Neither shall it be imputed unto him that offereth it” — imputation language in the law of leftovers.

pos: a. and n. (the ordinal of a hundred; used to date the flood by Noah's own years, and to name the monthly interest Nehemiah made the nobles restore)
etymology: From hundred — Old English hundred, from hund, a hundred, and raed, a reckoning — with the ordinal ending. The Hebrew at Nehemiah 5:11 is literally meath ha-keseph, the hundredth of the money.
biblical_def: Two very different uses. Genesis dates the flood by the years of one man: “Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth” (Genesis 7:6), and the drying is dated “in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month” (Genesis 8:13). Moses supplies day, month, and year throughout the account, which is not how legend is written. The other use is economic and is one of the sharpest scenes in the Old Testament. Nehemiah found that Jewish nobles were lending to their own brethren at interest during a famine and taking their fields, vineyards, and children in pledge. He assembled a great congregation against them and demanded restitution: “Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them” (Nehemiah 5:11). The hundredth part is generally understood as the monthly rate — one percent a month, twelve percent a year — and the law forbade any usury of a brother. They agreed, and Nehemiah took an oath of them (Nehemiah 5:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hundredth as the ordinal of a hundred, and as a noun one of a hundred equal parts.
webster_full: HUNDREDTH, a. The ordinal of a hundred.
HUNDRED, a. Denoting the product of ten multiplied by ten, or the number of ten times ten.
HUNDRED, n. A collection, consisting of ten times ten individuals or units.
USURY, n. Formerly, interest; or a premium given for the use of money.
2. In present usage, illegal interest; a premium or compensation paid for the use of money borrowed, beyond the rate of interest established by law.
scriptures: Genesis 7:6
And Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth.
Genesis 8:13

And it came to pass in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from off the earth: and Noah removed the covering of the ark, and looked, and, behold, the face of the ground was dry.
Nehemiah 5:11

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.
Nehemiah 5:12

Then said they, We will restore them, and will require nothing of them; so will we do as thou sayest. Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them, that they should do according to this promise.
corruption_summary: The flood dates are dismissed as invented precision, and the usury reform of Nehemiah 5 is treated as an economic policy rather than a covenant obligation.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 7 and 8 give the flood a calendar: the seventeenth day of the second month of Noah's six hundredth year for the beginning, the first day of the first month of his six hundred and first for the drying, the twenty-seventh day of the second month for the earth being dry. Critical readings treat this precision as a literary device of a later editor, and the whole narrative as a reworked Mesopotamian flood story. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and a historical worldwide flood, and observes that our Lord treated Noah's days as fact and as the pattern of His own coming, and that Peter twice grounds doctrine on the historicity of the ark and the eight souls saved by water.

Nehemiah 5 is more often skipped than denied, which is its own kind of loss. The nobles were doing something legal by every commercial standard of the ancient world and forbidden by the law of Moses, which prohibited taking usury of a brother. Nehemiah's argument is not economic efficiency but covenant identity — ought ye not to walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the heathen our enemies? — and he adds that he and his servants had lent money and corn and would likewise leave off. He required nothing of others that he had not first done himself, which is why the assembly said amen and praised the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew meah, a hundred — Genesis 8:13; meath ha-keseph, the hundredth of the money — Nehemiah 5:11; neshek, usury, literally a bite.
roots_lines: Hebrew meah — a hundred; the numeral behind both uses.
Hebrew meath ha-keseph — “the hundredth of the money”; Nehemiah 5:11, understood as the monthly rate.
Hebrew neshek — usury, literally a bite; the word of the Mosaic prohibition, Exodus 22:25.
Hebrew mashsha — a loan or exaction; Nehemiah 5:7, the charge against the nobles.
Old English hundred, from hund and raed, a reckoning — the source of the English word.
usage: “In the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day” — the flood dated by a man's years.
“Also the hundredth part of the money… that ye exact of them” — the interest restored.
“I called the priests, and took an oath of them” — Nehemiah did not trust the promise alone.

pos: n. (a portion regularly granted; once only, of the daily provision granted to Jehoiachin in Babylon — the last fact recorded in the books of Kings)
etymology: From Old French alouer, to place or assign, blended with Latin allaudare, to approve. The Hebrew at 2 Kings 25:30 is aruchah, an allotted ration or meal, from a root meaning to journey — provision measured out for the road.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it stands at the very end of the history of the kings of Judah: “And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life” (2 Kings 25:30). Jehoiachin had been carried to Babylon as a boy king, and after thirty-seven years in prison Evilmerodach “did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison”, spoke kindly to him, and “set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon” (2 Kings 25:28). His prison garments were changed and “he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life” (2 Kings 25:29). Jeremiah records the same closing scene (Jeremiah 52:34). It is a strange place for a history to end — not with restoration, not with a return, but with a captive king eating at a foreign table. The chronicler of Kings, writing to a people in exile, has deliberately left the reader with the one thing that remained: the line of David alive, out of prison, and fed. Matthew 1 lists Jechonias, and the genealogy runs on to Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines allowance as a portion appointed, a stated quantity, as of provisions or wages, and also permission or sanction.
webster_full: ALLOWANCE, n. The act of allowing or admitting.
2. Permission; license; approbation; sanction.
3. Admission; assent to a fact or state of things.
4. That which is allowed; a portion appointed; a stated quantity, as of food or drink; hence in general, abatement; as, to make allowance for the inexperience of youth.
ALLOW, v.t. To grant, give or yield; as, to allow a servant his wages.
scriptures: 2 Kings 25:30
And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
2 Kings 25:28
And he spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon;
2 Kings 25:29
And changed his prison garments: and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life.
Jeremiah 52:34
And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
corruption_summary: The ending of Kings is read as an anticlimax, when it is a deliberate and slender sign of a covenant God had not abandoned.
corruption_paragraphs: Commentators often call the close of 2 Kings anticlimactic or ambiguous, and treat it as the historian trailing off after the destruction of Jerusalem. Read against the covenant with David it is nothing of the sort. God had sworn that David would not want a man to sit upon the throne of Israel, and the last four chapters of Kings recount the systematic dismantling of everything that promise seemed to require — the city burnt, the temple stripped, the sons of Zedekiah killed before his eyes and his own eyes put out. And then, in four verses, an heir of David is brought out of a Babylonian prison, clothed, seated above other kings, and fed daily for life. The narrative does not comment. It does not need to.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how God's promises look while they are being kept. Nothing about Jehoiachin's daily ration resembled a throne in Jerusalem, and a reader in exile could be forgiven for seeing only a pensioned captive. Yet Haggai would address Zerubbabel his grandson as a signet, and Matthew would write Jechonias into the genealogy of Christ. The line held by a thread, and the thread was a daily allowance at a pagan table. That is very often the shape of providence, and the reason believers are told to walk by faith and not by sight.
roots_summary: Hebrew aruchah, an allotted ration — 2 Kings 25:30, Jeremiah 52:34; tamid, continual — the adjective attached to it; debar yom be-yomo, a daily rate.
roots_lines: Hebrew aruchah — an allowance, ration, allotted meal; 2 Kings 25:30 and Proverbs 15:17.
Hebrew tamid — continual, perpetual; the same word used of the continual burnt offering.
Hebrew debar yom be-yomo — a day's matter in its day; the phrase rendered “a daily rate.”
Hebrew nasa rosh — to lift up the head; 2 Kings 25:27, of Jehoiachin brought out of prison.
Old French alouer, to assign a place — the source of the English word.
usage: “A continual allowance… all the days of his life” — the last fact in the books of Kings.
“Set his throne above the throne of the kings” — a captive raised, and still a captive.
The line of David held by a thread, and the thread was a daily ration.

pos: v. (to set a valuation upon; the priest's office in Leviticus 27, where every vowed thing was appraised and the poor man's vow appraised by his ability)
etymology: From Latin aestimare, to value or appraise. The Hebrew is arak, to set in order or arrange, and so to fix a value; the related noun erek is the valuation itself, and both saturate Leviticus 27.
biblical_def: Leviticus 27 governs vows, and its machinery is valuation. “When a man shall sanctify his house to be holy unto the LORD, then the priest shall estimate it, whether it be good or bad: as the priest shall estimate it, so shall it stand” (Leviticus 27:14). A man might devote a person, a beast, a house, or a field to the LORD, and since the sanctuary could not use a house, a redemption price was fixed by the priest and the man paid it. The scale is given at the head of the chapter by age and sex, and it is the standard rate for such vows — not a valuation of the worth of a soul, which the same law elsewhere declares beyond price. Then comes the clause that shows the character of the legislation: “But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” (Leviticus 27:8). No man was to be shut out of a vow by poverty, and no man was to be ruined by one. The whole chapter assumes that a vow is serious, costly, and voluntary — and that God had rather a man be able to pay than make a grand promise he cannot keep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines estimate as to judge and form an opinion of the value of, to rate by judgment or opinion, to compute or calculate.
webster_full: ESTIMATE, v.t. To judge and form an opinion of the value of; to rate by judgment or opinion, without weighing or measuring.
It is sometimes used for esteem, to set a value on, as on a person.
2. To compute; to calculate; to reckon.
ESTIMATE, n. A valuing or rating in the mind; a judgment or opinion of the value, degree, extent or quantity of any thing.
ESTIMATION, n. The act of estimating. 2. Calculation; computation; an estimate.
scriptures: Leviticus 27:14
And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy unto the LORD, then the priest shall estimate it, whether it be good or bad: as the priest shall estimate it, so shall it stand.
Leviticus 27:2
Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation.
Leviticus 27:8
But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him.
Ecclesiastes 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 27's schedule of values is misread as pricing human beings, when it fixes redemption rates for vows and expressly bends them for the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: The valuation table of Leviticus 27 — so many shekels for a male between twenty and sixty, so many for a female, less for the very young and the very old — is frequently produced as evidence that Scripture prices people and prices women lower. The reading mistakes what the numbers do. These are not assessments of worth but standard redemption sums for a vow, calculated on the ordinary value of labour in an agrarian economy, which is why they fall for the very young and the aged of both sexes. The same law forbids taking any ransom for the life of a murderer, because a life cannot be paid for — the exact opposite of pricing souls.

The chapter's own clause about the poor settles the character of the legislation. If a man could not meet the standard sum, the priest was to value him according to his ability — a discretionary, downward, individual assessment, so that poverty never barred a man from consecrating himself. Read alongside Ecclesiastes 5:5 the doctrine is complete: a vow is not required, but a vow made must be paid, and God provides a lawful way for a poor man to make and discharge one. This is the same principle by which the law offered turtledoves where a lamb was beyond reach — and it is the offering Joseph and Mary brought.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak, to arrange, to set a value — Leviticus 27:8, 14; erek, the valuation itself — Leviticus 27:2; neder, a vow; Latin aestimare, to appraise.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak — to set in order, arrange, and so to appraise; the verb throughout Leviticus 27.
Hebrew erek — the estimation or valuation; the noun in Leviticus 27:2.
Hebrew neder — a vow; the voluntary undertaking the chapter regulates.
Hebrew hissig yad — the reach of the hand, one's ability; the basis of the poor man's valuation.
Latin aestimare, to value — the source of the English word and of esteem.
usage: “As the priest shall estimate it, so shall it stand” — the valuation was final.
“If he be poorer than thy estimation… according to his ability” — the rate bent for the poor.
“Better is it that thou shouldest not vow” — the whole chapter assumes a vow is costly.

pos: n. pl. (costs disbursed; twice in the decree of Darius, ordering the rebuilding of the temple to be paid for out of the king's own revenue)
etymology: From Latin expensa, money paid out, from expendere, to weigh out. The Aramaic at Ezra 6:4 is niphqa, outlay or expenditure, from a root meaning to go out — what goes out of the treasury.
biblical_def: Both occurrences fall in one of the most remarkable state papers in Scripture. The adversaries of Judah had written to Darius asking him to search the records and stop the building; Darius searched, found the decree of Cyrus, and issued his own. The original decree had specified: “With three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber: and let the expenses be given out of the king's house” (Ezra 6:4). Darius confirmed and enlarged it — the tribute beyond the river was to fund the work without delay, and beyond that the daily sacrifices were to be supplied at royal cost: “young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail” (Ezra 6:9). He closes with a curse on any king or people who should alter or destroy the house, and the words “I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed” (Ezra 6:12). A pagan emperor, answering a complaint intended to stop the work, funded it instead and threatened its enemies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expense as a laying out or expending, the disbursing of money, or the cost or charge incurred.
webster_full: EXPENSE, n. A laying out or expending; the disbursing of money, or the employment and consumption of any thing.
2. Money expended; cost; charge; that which is disbursed in payment or in charity.
Great expenses may be incurred without judgment or profit.
EXPEND, v.t. To lay out; to disburse; to spend.
EXPENSIVE, a. Costly; requiring much expense.
scriptures: Ezra 6:4
With three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber: and let the expenses be given out of the king's house:
Ezra 6:9

And that which they have need of, both young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail:
Ezra 6:12

And the God that hath caused his name to dwell there destroy all kings and people, that shall put to their hand to alter and to destroy this house of God which is at Jerusalem. I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed.
Proverbs 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
corruption_summary: The episode is read as a lucky administrative outcome, when Ezra presents it as the LORD turning the heart of an emperor.
corruption_paragraphs: A purely political reading of Ezra 6 is available and is often taken: Persian imperial policy favoured local cults for reasons of stability, Darius was consolidating a contested throne, and the decree served his interests. All of that may be true and none of it touches Ezra's claim. Scripture regularly shows God working through the ordinary calculations of statesmen without those calculations ceasing to be genuine — Cyrus is called the LORD's anointed and His shepherd, and told that God girded him though he had not known Him. Proverbs states the doctrine as a rule: the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.

The pastoral use is in the shape of the answer. The enemies of the work wrote to the king in order to stop it, and the letter they sent produced a search of the archives, the recovery of a forgotten decree, imperial funding, a daily supply for the sacrifices, and a royal curse on anyone who interfered. God did not merely thwart the opposition; He made the opposition's own instrument the means of the supply. Joseph's brothers sold him into the position that saved them; Haman built the gallows; the crucifixion was the determinate counsel of God carried out by wicked hands. Ezra 6 belongs to that pattern, and the elders builded and prospered.
roots_summary: Aramaic niphqa, outlay or expense — Ezra 6:4, 6:8; beth malka, the king's house; teem, a decree — Ezra 6:12; Latin expendere, to weigh out.
roots_lines: Aramaic niphqa — expenditure, outlay; Ezra 6:4 and 6:8, of the royal funding.
Aramaic teem — a decree or edict; “I Darius have made a decree.”
Aramaic osparna — speedily, diligently, without fail; the recurring adverb of the decree.
Hebrew leb melek — the king's heart; Proverbs 21:1, in the hand of the LORD.
Latin expendere, to weigh out — the source of the English word.
usage: “Let the expenses be given out of the king's house” — Cyrus's forgotten decree, recovered.
“Let it be given them day by day without fail” — the sacrifices funded by an emperor.
The letter sent to stop the work became the means of paying for it.

pos: n. (the dealing out of goods to those in need; of the Jerusalem church's care of its poor, and of the Corinthian collection Paul gathered for famine relief)
etymology: From Latin distribuere, to deal out, from dis- and tribuere, to assign. The Greek at Acts 4:35 is diadidomi, to give out among; at 2 Corinthians 9:13 the word is koinonia, fellowship — the sharing itself.
biblical_def: Luke describes the practice of the Jerusalem church in terms that have been misread in every century since. Possessors of lands or houses sold them and brought the prices, “And laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need” (Acts 4:35), with the result stated first: “Neither was there any among them that lacked” (Acts 4:34). Four features govern the account. The selling was voluntary — Peter tells Ananias that the land was his own and the price was in his own power. It was occasional, not a permanent surrender of all property, since believers still met in houses. It was administered by the apostles and soon delegated to deacons. And the measure was need. Paul's word for the same thing among the Gentile churches is koinonia: “for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” (2 Corinthians 9:13), and he notes that the recipients glorify God for it. The command to the rich is put in the same register: “that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate” (1 Timothy 6:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines distribution as the act of dividing among a number, dealing out in parts or portions — and in a scriptural sense, the giving of alms.
webster_full: DISTRIBUTION, n. The act of dividing among a number; a dealing in parts or portions.
2. The act of giving in charity; the bestowment of alms.
3. Dispensation; administration to numbers.
DISTRIBUTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to give or bestow in parts or portions.
COMMUNICATE, v.i. To share with others; to impart a portion of what one has.
scriptures: Acts 4:34
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
Acts 4:35
And laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need.
2 Corinthians 9:13
Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men;
1 Timothy 6:18
That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
corruption_summary: Acts 4 is claimed as a mandate for compulsory collectivism on one side and explained away entirely on the other; the text supports neither.
corruption_paragraphs: The passage has been enlisted for two centuries as scriptural warrant for common ownership imposed by authority, and the enlistment fails on Peter's own words to Ananias: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? The sin was the lie, not the withholding, and the question presupposes a right of private property that the apostle does not dispute. Nor did the practice abolish households; the church continued to meet from house to house, and Mary the mother of John Mark still had a home in Jerusalem in chapter twelve. What is described is voluntary, occasional, need-measured liquidation by believers under extraordinary pressure, administered by the church for its own poor.

The opposite error is to explain the chapter away so thoroughly that nothing is required of anyone. Luke states the outcome as a commendation: neither was there any among them that lacked, and he says it twice in two chapters. Paul organised a transcontinental collection over years, carried it with a delegation so that no man could suspect the handling, and described its aim as an equality — that the abundance of one might supply the want of another. A congregation in which members lack necessities while others have abundance has not preserved a doctrine of property; it has failed a plain apostolic standard.
roots_summary: Greek diadidomi, to distribute — Acts 4:35; koinonia, fellowship, sharing — 2 Corinthians 9:13; eumetadotos, ready to distribute — 1 Timothy 6:18.
roots_lines: Greek diadidomi — to give out among, distribute; Acts 4:35.
Greek koinonia — fellowship, communion, and so a contribution shared; 2 Corinthians 9:13.
Greek eumetadotos — ready to impart; 1 Timothy 6:18, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek koinonikos — willing to communicate, sociable in giving; the companion word in the same verse.
Greek chreia — need; Acts 4:35, the measure of the distribution.
usage: “Distribution was made unto every man according as he had need” — need was the measure.
“Neither was there any among them that lacked” — the outcome Luke commends.
“Ready to distribute, willing to communicate” — the charge to the rich.

pos: n. (the place of receiving; in all three Gospels, the tax booth from which Matthew rose and followed Christ)
etymology: From Latin recepta, things received, through Old French recete — the p was inserted later in imitation of the Latin and was never sounded. The Greek phrase is telonion, the tax-office or toll booth, from telos, a tax.
biblical_def: The word occurs three times and always in the same phrase, the receipt of custom — the booth where tolls were collected on goods passing through. Matthew records his own call in the third person: “as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him” (Matthew 9:9). Mark and Luke give the man his other name: “he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom” (Mark 2:14); “saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom” (Luke 5:27). Luke adds the detail that makes the call cost something: “And he left all, rose up, and followed him” (Luke 5:28). The fishermen could return to their nets and did, after the crucifixion; a tax farmer who walked away from his booth could never have it back, since the franchise would be sold to another man that week. Of all the disciples, Matthew burned the most decisively. He then made Christ a great feast in his own house and filled it with publicans, which is the first thing he did with what he had left.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines receipt as the act of receiving, the place of receiving, and a written acknowledgment of something received — citing the receipt of custom.
webster_full: RECEIPT, n. The act of receiving; as, the receipt of a letter.
2. The place of receiving; as the receipt of custom. Matt. 9.
3. A writing acknowledging the taking of money or goods.
4. Reception; admission.
CUSTOM, n. Tribute, toll or tax paid to the sovereign on goods imported or exported.
scriptures: Matthew 9:9
And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
Mark 2:14
And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him.
Luke 5:27
And after these things he went forth, and saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said unto him, Follow me.
Luke 5:28
And he left all, rose up, and followed him.
corruption_summary: The call is softened into an invitation Matthew considered, when all three Gospels record a command obeyed on the spot at unrecoverable cost.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern presentations of conversion make the sinner the deciding party: Christ offers, the man weighs it, and at length he accepts. The three accounts of Matthew's call read otherwise. Christ passes by, sees the man, says two words, and the man rises. There is no recorded deliberation, no interval, and nothing in the text about Matthew's prior interest. What is described is an effectual call — a summons that carries its own power to be obeyed — and it is the ordinary New Testament pattern, from Lazarus at the tomb to Saul on the road. Reformed theology did not invent that doctrine; it read it out of scenes like this one.

The cost is easy to miss and Luke will not let it be missed: he left all. A tax booth was a purchased franchise on a trade route, and a man who walked away from it at midday had no way back. Matthew is also the disciple who, having lost his income, gave a great feast — and filled the guest list with the only society he had, publicans and sinners, so that the Pharisees complained and our Lord answered that the whole need no physician. The first act of the man who left all was to spend what remained on getting his old associates into a room with Christ.
roots_summary: Greek telonion, the tax booth — Matthew 9:9, Mark 2:14, Luke 5:27; telones, a publican; akoloutheo, to follow — the verb of the response.
roots_lines: Greek telonion — the toll-house or tax booth; the phrase “the receipt of custom” in all three Gospels.
Greek telones — a tax collector, publican; Luke 5:27 of Levi.
Greek akoloutheo — to follow, accompany as a disciple; the verb in every account.
Greek anistemi — to rise up; “he arose, and followed him.”
Latin recepta, things received — the source of the English word; the p was never sounded.
usage: “Sitting at the receipt of custom” — the tax booth on the trade route.
“He arose, and followed him” — no recorded deliberation, and no way back.
“He left all” — and then spent what remained on a feast for publicans.
